--- title: "R" subtitle: "Extended course – day 1" format: revealjs # Session 4 of day 1 of the Extended course, the same for every case: R taught # live in the IDE, on the housing-audit file, which the modules on the tools # use as their running example. Four sections: objects and data frames, # packages and the data, the pipe and the verbs, shares, a table and a figure. # Three optional slides stay on the d toggle (run "r"): the programming # languages, the package layer and the two ways to count the emails. core-runs: [] --- ## {#overview .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.todaymeta} Session 4 of 6 on day 1, the same for every case ::: :::: {.todaybox} ::: {.nonincremental .fs-85} 1. Objects and data frames – the console and the script, objects and vectors, missing values, and a table of data 2. Packages and the data – installing and calling a package, then reading the housing-audit file and looking at it 3. The pipe and the verbs – the steps of a calculation in their order, and the datawizard verbs that filter, select, change and summarise 4. Shares, a table and a figure – the share of replies that greeted the sender by name, a difference in shares, a first table and a first figure ::: :::: ::: {.todaytake .fs-85} You leave able to read a data file into R, reshape it with a handful of verbs, and set a result out as a table and as a figure ::: ::: {.todaymeta} Type along in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), in the workspace of the housing-audit case ::: ::: notes The afternoon turns to the tools of the course, and we start with R. You worked through the module Getting started with R before the course, in your browser, so very little of this will be new. What changes is the place: from now on every line runs in your IDE, on your own machine, and on one file, the data of the housing-audit case, whatever the case of your course. I type on the shared screen and you type the same lines on yours. The session has four sections. Objects and data frames come first, then packages and the reading of the file, then the pipe and the verbs of datawizard, and last the three things that the course asks of R most often: a difference between two shares, a table and a figure. Each section ends with a short task of your own. ::: ## Programming languages {#languages-what-you-are-actually-choosing .deepdive run="r"} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
RBuilt by statisticians for data analysis. Hard to beat for models, tables and figures, through its packages.
PythonA general language that also does data. Better for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning.
JuliaFast and young, with few packages. Worth it when a model takes hours.
StataExcellent panel and survey estimators, superb documentation, one syntax. Costs money and keeps its source closed.
::: ::: {.fragment .small .fs-80} You do not have to choose once and for all. Quarto runs R, Python and Julia chunks in the **same document**, and the blocks of the module Getting started with R run a copy of R built to work inside a web page. ::: ::: notes A slower look at the languages, because people agonise about this and mostly need not. R was built by statisticians for data analysis, and that is still where it is strongest, in models, tables and figures, largely through its packages: whatever estimator your literature uses, somebody has probably written the package for it. Python is a general-purpose language that also does data, so it is the better choice for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning. Julia is fast and young, with few packages, and earns its place when a model takes hours rather than seconds. Stata deserves respect, with excellent panel and survey estimators, the best documentation in the business and one consistent syntax, but it costs money and its source is closed. None of this is a choice for life, since Quarto runs R, Python and Julia chunks in one document. ::: ## Open-source software {#what-open-source-buys-you .smaller} ::: {.small} - **You can read it.** The source of `lm()`, of `glm()`, of every package that this course loads, is public, so no estimator has to be taken on trust - **No licence stands between a reader and your analysis.** Anyone, anywhere, can run your code without buying anything - **It outlives your institution.** A licence expires when you change job; a package on CRAN does not - **You can fix it, and so can others.** Bugs get found because thousands of people run the same code on different data ::: ::: {.fragment .small} With a proprietary toolchain, **the price of reproducing your work falls on your reader**, who has to buy the licence. ::: ::: notes Stata is proprietary and R is open source, and that difference matters for reproduction. There are four reasons, and only one of them is money. First, you can read it. You can go and look at the source of any function we run in this course, so you never have to take an estimator on trust. Second, and this is the one that bears on our subject, no licence stands between a reader and your analysis. If your replication package needs a licence they do not have, your work is not reproducible for them, however carefully you wrote it. Third, it outlives your institution – a site licence ends when you change job, and a package on CRAN does not. Fourth, bugs get found, because thousands of people run the same code against different data. On money, the question is who pays. Reproducibility has a price, and a proprietary toolchain hands that price to your reader. ::: ## The workspace {#the-workspace .smaller} ::: {.small} - Every step of the afternoon runs in the **workspace of the housing-audit case**, the folder `replication-lab-housing-main`, whatever the case of your course - Open the folder itself, not a file inside it: **File → Open Folder…** in Positron and VS Code, or the file `replication-lab-housing.Rproj` in RStudio - Then open a new R script, save it in that folder, and type each step of this session into it ::: ::: {.fragment .small} If the folder is not on your machine yet, its zip is on the setup page, in step 4, under the tab Housing audit. ::: ::: {.urlbox .fragment} [[codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html#the-workspace](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html#the-workspace)]{.fs-70} ::: ::: notes Before anybody types, the folder. Every step this afternoon runs in the workspace of the housing-audit case, because the modules on the tools use it as their running example, whatever the case of your course. If your course works on that case, you installed the folder before the course and ran its check script. If it works on another case, the folder that you installed belongs to that case, and the housing-audit folder is one more zip from the same page. Open the folder itself rather than a file inside it, because R then works in that folder, and the path to the data in the second section finds the file. Then open a new script, save it in the folder under a name of your choice, and type into it as I type into mine. [advance] The address of the setup page is on the screen. ::: # Objects and data frames {#objects-and-data-frames .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 1 ::: ::: notes Section one starts at the very bottom, with the places where you type R and the way in which R answers. Then come the two pieces from which everything else is built: objects, which give a value a name, and vectors, which hold a run of values. One small fact about vectors carries most of the arithmetic of the course, that the mean of a run of ones and zeros is a share. We end with the data frame, the table in which R keeps a dataset, and with a first task of your own. ::: ## The console and the script {#the-console-and-the-script .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r 1014 - 23 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 991 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} - **The console** runs a line as soon as you press Enter, and keeps no record of how a result was reached - **A script** is a plain text file ending in `.R`. Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) sends the line under the cursor to the console, and the script keeps the line - Try things in the console, and move anything that matters into the script ::: ::: notes In your IDE there are two places to type R. The console runs a line the moment you press Enter. Type one thousand and fourteen minus twenty-three, and R answers nine hundred and ninety-one, the emails that reached a housing authority out of the thousand and fourteen that were sent. The one in square brackets is not part of the answer, because R numbers the values that it prints. [advance] A script keeps what you type. Put the same line in your new script, leave the cursor on it, and press Control and Enter: the line goes to the console and runs there. [advance] The rule of the course is to try things in the console and to move anything that matters into the script, because the script records how a result was reached, and the console forgets it when the session ends. ::: ## Objects and vectors {#objects-and-vectors .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r emails_sent <- 1014 # a number first_name <- "Santiago" # text, called a character string, in quotes emails_sent - 23 delivered <- c(308, 326, 357) # white, Black and Hispanic names replies <- c(177, 198, 188) replies / delivered # one division for each group ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 991 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5746753 0.6073620 0.5266106 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} `<-` gives a value a name, and the name then stands in for the value. `c()` combines values of one type into a **vector**, and arithmetic works on a whole vector at once. ::: ::: notes R works by putting values into named objects. The arrow, typed as a less-than sign and a hyphen, assigns: emails sent gets one thousand and fourteen, and from then on the name stands in for the number, so emails sent minus twenty-three gives nine hundred and ninety-one again. Names are case-sensitive, and asking for a name that was never assigned gives the message "object not found", which you will meet whenever a line uses an object that an earlier line was meant to make. A vector is a run of values of one type, made with c, for combine. These two hold, for the white, the Black and the Hispanic names in turn, the emails that reached an official and the replies that came back, and one division gives the three reply rates. The six numbers were typed by hand, and the third section computes them from the file. ::: ## Means and missing values {#means-and-missing-values .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r greeted <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0) # five replies, 1 = opened with the name of the sender mean(greeted) # the share of 1s greeted <- c(1, 0, NA, 1, 0) # the third reply carries no greeting code mean(greeted) mean(greeted, na.rm = TRUE) # the share among the four replies with a code ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The file has missing values of three kinds: the 23 emails that bounced have no reply, an email without a reply has no greeting, and 5 replies were never coded. The course never uses `na.rm = TRUE` without saying which rows it removes. ::: ::: notes One small fact carries most of the arithmetic of the course. When a vector holds only ones and zeros, its mean is the share of ones, because the mean adds the values, which counts the ones, and divides the sum by the number of values. The outcome of the claim of the housing-audit case, whether a reply opened with the name of the sender, is stored in exactly this way, so the share of replies that greeted the sender by name is a mean. Real data have gaps, which R marks NA, for not available, and any calculation that meets one returns NA, because the answer cannot be known. The argument na dot rm removes the missing values first. [advance] In our file a missing value can mean three different things, and deciding what to do with each kind is part of the analysis. ::: ## Data frames {#data-frames .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r emails <- tibble::tibble( name = c("Brett", "Santiago", "Emily"), reply = c(1, 1, 0), named = c(1, 0, NA) ) emails emails$named # one column, as a vector ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 name reply named 1 Brett 1 1 2 Santiago 1 0 3 Emily 0 NA ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 0 NA ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} A **data frame** is a table: vectors of equal length standing side by side as columns, with one row for each observation. A **tibble** is a data frame that prints its size and the type of each column, `` for text and `` for numbers. ::: ::: notes A data frame is how R stores a table: vectors of the same length standing side by side as columns, with one row for each observation, and almost everything in the course is a data frame. This one is built by hand, with three emails, the name that signed each, whether a reply came and whether the reply greeted the sender by name. The third email shows why a greeting can be missing: no reply came, so there was no greeting to code. The part before the two colons names the package from which the function comes, which the next section explains. A tibble prints its size on the first line and the type of each column under its name. The dollar sign pulls one column out as a vector, which is often the quickest way to look at a single column, and for reshaping a table the course uses the verbs of the third section. ::: ## Hands-on 1 – The reply rate {#hands-on-1-the-reply-rate .smaller} ::: {.small} In your script, with the two vectors of the last slides: ::: ::: {.fs-130} ```r sum(replies) / sum(______) replies[3] Emails_sent ``` ::: ::: {.small} 1. Fill the blank so that the line divides all the replies by all the delivered emails, which gives the share of the delivered emails that drew a reply, whatever the name 2. Square brackets pick out a value by its position: the third is the replies to the Hispanic names 3. A capital E makes another name: read what R says ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The share is 0.568113, the reply rate of the 991 delivered emails, which the second section reaches again from the file. ::: ::: notes Your turn, on your own machine, with three short lines in your script. First, fill the blank so that the line divides all the replies by all the delivered emails, which gives the share of the delivered emails that drew a reply, whatever the name that signed each email. Second, pick out the third value of the replies with square brackets, the replies to the Hispanic names. Third, type the name of the first object with a capital E and read what R says, because you will meet that message many times, and it always means that R has no object of that name in the session. Take the time you need, and if a line stops with an error that you cannot read, tell me. [advance] The share is a little under fifty-seven per cent, and we will reach it again from the file. ::: # Packages and the data {#packages-and-the-data .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 2 ::: ::: notes Section two brings in the data. First the packages, the bundles of functions written by other people on which nearly all of the work depends, with the two steps of using one and the two error messages that go with those steps. Then we read the housing-audit file into R and look at it, first as a whole and then column by column, before any analysis touches it. The section ends with a task that counts the replies by the kind of address to which each email went. ::: ## Packages {#packages .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r install.packages("pak") # once on a new machine pak::pak("readr") # step 1: install a package, once readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv") # step 2: call a function by its # package and its name ``` ::: ::: {.small} - **Install** a package once on each machine, with `pak::pak()`. The check script of the workspace prints the line that installs whatever its exercise needs and you lack - **Call** every function that does not come with R as `package::function()`, so that each line says where its functions come from ::: ::: {.fragment .small} | R says | It means | |---|---| | `there is no package called 'readr'` | Step 1 never happened on this machine: install the package | | `could not find function "read_csv"` | The function was called without its package, and no `library()` line attached the package | ::: ::: notes Everything that we typed so far comes with R itself, apart from tibble, which came from a package. Packages are bundles of functions with their documentation, published on CRAN, the archive of R packages, and using one takes two steps, a difference that trips nearly every newcomer at least once. Step one installs the package on your machine, once, and the course does it with pak, a package that installs other packages. The check script of your workspace prints the line that installs every package that its exercise needs and that you lack. Step two is the call itself, and the course writes every function that does not come with R as the name of its package, two colons and the name of the function, so that anyone reading a line can tell where it comes from. [advance] The two messages that you will meet most often come from these two steps. ::: ## The package layer {#the-package-layer .deepdive run="r"} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
easystatsData work with datawizard, and model output as tidy data: parameters, performance, effect sizes.
tidyverseReading files, and the verbs that datawizard lacks. One grammar across all of it.
modelsummaryRegression tables ready to publish, built from the fitted models.
marginaleffectsPredictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model.
::: ::: {.fragment .small .fs-80} The figures of the course come from **`tinyplot`**, its tables from **`tinytable`**, and the causal graphs of the second day from **`dagitty`**. The setup page lists the packages of each workspace, and the check script of the workspace reports any that are missing. ::: ::: notes A word about packages, because this is where the advantage of R lies. Easystats comes first in this course. Its datawizard package does the data work, filtering, selecting and summarising, and the rest of the family turns the output of a model back into tidy data, coefficients, fit statistics and effect sizes, instead of the block of printed text that summary gives you. The tidyverse reads the files and covers the few verbs that datawizard lacks. Modelsummary builds regression tables ready for a journal straight from the fitted models, so the table cannot disagree with the model. And marginaleffects computes predictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model, which is how you get from a coefficient to a statement in the units in which your reader thinks. The figures of the course come from tinyplot, the tables from tinytable and the causal graphs from dagitty. ::: ## Reading the file {#reading-the-file .smaller} ::: {.small} One row for each of the 1,014 emails that the original authors (OAs) of a field experiment sent in 2014 to public housing authorities in the United States, each signed with one of six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. ::: ::: {.fs-130} ```r audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 1014 Columns: 16 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (10): name, group, name_sex, waitlist, white_third, blac... dbl (6): email_id, hard_email, reply, reply24, named, hispa... ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The path is relative to the folder of the workspace, so the line runs on any machine on which the folder is open. The scripts of the workspace add `show_col_types = FALSE`, which keeps the report on the columns quiet. ::: ::: notes Now the data: one row for each email of the field experiment run by the original authors, the OAs, in which emails signed with names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant went to public housing authorities in the United States. The file is a CSV, short for comma-separated values, a plain-text table with one line for each row and commas between the columns, which any program can open. In the module, in your browser, you read it with read dot csv, which comes with R. In your IDE the course reads it with read underscore csv from readr, which treats an empty cell as missing without being told, and reports what it read: a thousand and fourteen rows, sixteen columns, and the type of each. [advance] The path is relative, so R looks for the file in the folder in which it works, which is the folder of the workspace once you have opened it. ::: ## A first look {#a-first-look .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="38%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```r nrow(audit) datawizard::data_peek(audit) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1014 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} The first question to ask of any dataset is what a row is. Here a row is one email, and the codebook beside the file in `data/` describes every column. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="62%"} ::: {.fs-90} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Data frame with 1014 rows and 16 variables Variable | Type | Values -------------------------------------------------------- email_id | numeric | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, ... name | character | Shanice, Brett, ... group | character | black, white, black, ... name_sex | character | female, male, ... hard_email | numeric | 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, ... reply | numeric | 0, 1, 1, 1, NA, 1, ... reply24 | numeric | NA, 1, 1, 0, NA, 1, ... named | numeric | NA, 0, 1, 0, NA, 1, ... hispanic_official | numeric | NA, 1, 0, 0, NA, 1, ... waitlist | character | NA, 6, NA, NA, NA, ... white_third | character | top, middle, middle, ... black_third | character | lower, lower, ... hispanic_third | character | lower, top, top, ... pop_third | character | middle, lower, top, ... poverty_third | character | lower, middle, ... assessment_third | character | middle, top, lower, ... ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: notes Before any analysis, look at what you have, and the first question to ask of any dataset is what a row is. Here a row is one email. nrow counts the rows, a thousand and fourteen. data peek, from datawizard, turns the table on its side, with one line for each column, its type and its first values, so that all sixteen columns fit on the screen. Notice that reply already shows an NA among its first values: that email bounced and never reached an official. Every column is described in the codebook that sits beside the file in the data folder of the workspace, and a codebook is the second thing to read after any import. Your IDE can also show the data as a spreadsheet, with View of audit, and the next session spends some time in that viewer. ::: ## Counting values {#counting-values .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```r datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "reply") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` reply (reply) # total N=1014 valid N=991 Value | N | Raw % | Valid % | Cumulative % ------+-----+-------+---------+------------- 0 | 428 | 42.21 | 43.19 | 43.19 1 | 563 | 55.52 | 56.81 | 100.00 | 23 | 2.27 | | ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```r datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "named", by = "reply") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` named | 0 | 1 | | Total ------+-----+-----+------+------ 0 | 0 | 264 | 0 | 264 1 | 0 | 294 | 0 | 294 | 428 | 5 | 23 | 456 ------+-----+-----+------+------ Total | 428 | 563 | 23 | 1014 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: {.fragment .small} 1,014 emails, 23 bounced, 991 delivered, 563 replies, and 558 replies with a greeting code: the counts from which every analysis of the case starts. ::: ::: notes data tabulate counts the rows for each value of a column. For reply it gives the emails without a reply, the emails with one, and twenty-three NA, the emails that bounced. The column of valid percentages leaves the bounced emails out, so fifty-six point eight per cent is the reply rate among the delivered emails. On the right, the greeting tabulated by the reply explains every missing value in the outcome, if you read it a column at a time. An email without a reply, under the zero, has no greeting. A reply, under the one, carries a greeting code of one or zero, except for five replies that nobody coded. A bounced email has neither. In the console these tables print as text, where the module set them out as formatted tables on the page. [advance] These are the counts from which every analysis of the case starts. ::: ## Hands-on 2 – The harder addresses {#hands-on-2-the-harder-addresses .smaller} ::: {.small} `hard_email` is 1 where the address of the authority could not be found quickly on its own website and was taken from the list kept by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), and 0 otherwise. ::: ::: {.fs-130} ```r datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "reply", by = "______") ``` ::: ::: {.small} Fill the blank, run the line, and work out from the counts whether the harder addresses replied less often. ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Of the 445 delivered emails sent to a harder address, 217 drew a reply, against 346 of the 546 sent to an address found on the website of the authority. ::: ::: notes Your turn again. The column hard email marks the authorities whose address could not be found quickly on their own website and was taken instead from the list kept by the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Fill the blank so that the line tabulates the replies by that column, then read the counts and decide whether the harder addresses replied less often. The table counts emails rather than giving rates, so you will have to add up two cells in each column of the delivered emails, and the next section computes the rates for you. Take the time you need. [advance] Just under half of the delivered emails sent to a harder address drew a reply, against 63 per cent of the others. ::: # The pipe and the verbs {#the-pipe-and-the-verbs .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 3 ::: ::: notes Section three is about reshaping a table, which is most of the work after reading the data, and which almost always comes as a sequence of steps. The pipe lets you write those steps from top to bottom, in the order in which they happen. Then come the verbs of datawizard, one for each common operation on a table, all of which take a data frame and return one, so that they can be chained. By the end of the section you will have computed from the file the six numbers that we typed by hand in the first section. ::: ## The pipe {#the-pipe .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r round(mean(audit$reply, na.rm = TRUE), 3) # read from the inside out audit$reply |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) |> round(3) # read from left to right ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.568 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.568 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} `|>` passes whatever stands on its left as the first argument of the function on its right, so a chain reads as a list of steps, each joined to the next by 'then'. The older pipe `%>%`, from the magrittr package, does the same in code written before 2021, when `|>` became part of R. ::: ::: notes The pipe makes a sequence of steps readable. The first line takes the mean of the reply column, leaving out the bounced emails, and rounds it to three decimals, with each function wrapped inside the next, so you read it from the inside out. The second line does the same from left to right: take the column, then take its mean, then round it. Both give point five six eight, the reply rate that the table of the last section gave as a percentage. On one short line the gain is small, but it grows with every step of the chains that follow, which is why nearly all modern R is written this way. You will meet the older pipe in code written by others: read the two in the same way, and write the native one, as all the materials of the course do. ::: ## Rows and columns {#rows-and-columns .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |> datawizard::data_select(select = c("name", "group", "reply", "named")) |> datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = group == "hispanic") |> head() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 5 name group reply named hispanic_name 1 Shanice black 0 NA FALSE 2 Brett white 1 0 FALSE 3 Shanice black 1 1 FALSE 4 Tyrone black 1 0 FALSE 5 Gabriela hispanic 1 1 TRUE 6 Shanice black 0 NA FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} `data_filter()` keeps rows, `data_select()` keeps columns, `data_modify()` makes a column. The operators of a condition: `==` equals, `!=` does not equal, `%in%` is one of, `!` not, `&` and, and `is.na()` asks whether a value is missing. ::: ::: notes Three verbs from datawizard, chained with the pipe, which you read downwards as a sentence. Take the emails, then keep the rows that have a reply status, the delivered ones, then keep four columns, then make a new column that is true for the Hispanic names, then show the first six rows. data filter takes a condition, and the operators of a condition are worth learning together: two equals signs for equals, because one sign assigns, an exclamation mark for not, percent in percent for is one of, and is dot na for is missing. data select takes the names of the columns, in quotes. data modify makes a column from the columns that exist. Each verb takes a data frame and hands one back, which is what lets the verbs be chained, and the first row shows an email that drew no reply, so its greeting is missing. ::: ## Summaries by group {#summaries-by-group .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |> datawizard::data_summary( delivered = n(), replies = sum(reply), reply_rate = mean(reply), by = "group" ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` group | delivered | replies | reply_rate ------------------------------------------- black | 326 | 198 | 0.61 hispanic | 357 | 188 | 0.53 white | 308 | 177 | 0.57 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} `data_summary()` collapses many rows into one row of summaries, and with `by` into one row for each group; `n()` counts the rows of a group. These are the six numbers typed by hand in the first section. ::: ::: notes data summary is the verb that answers most of the questions that you will put to a dataset. It collapses many rows into one row of summaries, and with by, into one row for each group. Inside it, n counts the rows of a group, and sum and mean work as they did on a vector. Read the chain aloud: take the emails, keep the delivered ones, and for each group of names report three numbers. These are the six numbers that we typed by hand in the first section, now computed from the file, and the reply rates agree with the division that we did there. Two details are worth knowing. The groups come out in alphabetical order, and the rates print to two decimals while the table keeps every digit, so a number is rounded only when you round it, with round or in a formatted table. ::: ## Hands-on 3 – The reply rate by name {#hands-on-3-the-reply-rate-by-name .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |> datawizard::data_summary( delivered = n(), replies = sum(reply), reply_rate = mean(reply), by = "______" ) ``` ::: ::: {.small} 1. Fill the blank so that the chain summarises the delivered emails by the name that signed each, and find the name with the lowest reply rate 2. Then put `"hard_email"` in the blank, and compare the two rates with your counts from Hands-on 2 ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Santiago has the lowest reply rate, 0.52 of 202 delivered emails. By address, the rate is 0.63 for the addresses found on the websites and 0.49 for those taken from the list kept by HUD. ::: ::: notes Your turn. Edit the chain that you typed, or copy it, and fill the blank so that it summarises the delivered emails by the name that signed each email rather than by the group of the name, then find the name with the lowest reply rate. Then put hard email in the blank, run the chain again, and compare the two rates with the counts that you added up by hand in the second task. That is a habit worth keeping: a number reached in two ways, by two different pieces of code, is a number that you can rely on. Take the time you need. [advance] Santiago has the lowest reply rate, just below Gabriela, the other Hispanic name, and the rates by address agree with the counts of the second task. ::: # Shares, a table and a figure {#shares-a-table-and-a-figure .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 4 ::: ::: notes Section four puts the pieces together on the claim of the case. The claim compares two shares, so we compute both and the difference between them, the number that the housing-audit case calls its reference specification, against which every other analysis of the claim is compared. Then the two forms in which a result leaves R for a reader: a table, formatted with tinytable, the table package of the course, and a figure, drawn with tinyplot. The last slide of the section gathers the error messages that you are most likely to meet. ::: ## A difference in shares {#a-difference-in-shares .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r shares <- audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |> datawizard::data_summary(replies = n(), greeted = sum(named), share = mean(named), by = "group") shares shares |> datawizard::data_summary( gap_points = 100 * (share[group == "hispanic"] - share[group == "white"]) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` group | replies | greeted | share ------------------------------------ hispanic | 187 | 77 | 0.41 white | 175 | 107 | 0.61 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gap_points ---------- -19.97 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .small} A gap of −19.97 percentage points, the raw difference behind the shares of 61% and 41% reported by the OAs. The published estimate of −20.0 points comes from a logistic regression with covariates. ::: ::: notes The claim of the housing-audit case is that replies to emails signed with Hispanic names were less likely to greet the sender by name than replies to emails signed with white names. In the terms of the first section, that is a comparison of two means of a column of ones and zeros, so you already have every tool that it needs. The chain keeps the replies that carry a greeting code, from the white and the Hispanic names, and summarises the greeting in each group: sixty-one per cent of the replies to white names opened with the name of the sender, against forty-one per cent of the replies to Hispanic names. Inside data summary, square brackets pick out the value of one group, and multiplying by a hundred gives the difference in percentage points. [advance] The published estimate comes from another calculation, and the two agree closely. ::: ## Two ways to count {#two-ways-to-count .smaller .deepdive run="r"} ::: {.fs-130} ```r audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |> datawizard::data_modify(greeted = dplyr::if_else(reply == 1, named, 0)) |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(greeted)) |> datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), share = mean(greeted), by = "group") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` group | emails | share ------------------------- hispanic | 356 | 0.22 white | 306 | 0.35 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} Among every delivered email, a missing reply counting as no greeting by name, the gap is −13.34 points. Among the replies, the comparison asks whether the officials who replied wrote differently to the two groups of names; among all delivered emails, whether the name changed the chance of a reply that greeted the sender by name at all. ::: ::: notes That gap is counted among the replies only, because an email that drew no reply has no greeting. The other way to count keeps every delivered email and treats a missing reply as a reply without a greeting by name. if else, from dplyr, makes that column, keeping the greeting code where reply is one and putting zero elsewhere, and a second filter removes the five uncoded replies. Counted this way, the gap is 13.3 points instead of twenty. The two numbers answer two questions. Among the replies, did the officials who answered write differently to the two groups of names? Among all delivered emails, did the name change the chance of receiving a greeting by name at all, which mixes the decision to reply with the tone of the reply? In the housing-audit case, no other choice moves the estimate as far as this one. ::: ## Hands-on 4 – Black and white names {#hands-on-4-black-and-white-names .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named), group %in% c("white", "______")) |> datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group") |> datawizard::data_summary( gap_points = 100 * (share[group == "black"] - share[group == "white"]) ) ``` ::: ::: {.small} Fill the blank so that the chain computes the same gap, between the Black and the white names, among the coded replies. The column `group` spells the three groups in lower case. ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The gap is −5.02 points, a quarter of the gap between the Hispanic and the white names. Between the two male names, Santiago and Brett, it is −23.27 points, on 105 and 96 coded replies. ::: ::: notes Your turn, with the last task of the session. Fill the blank so that the chain computes the same gap, between the Black and the white names, among the coded replies. This chain does in one go what took two steps on the slide before: the first summary gives the two shares, and the second works on the table that the first returned and gives their difference. If you finish early, change the chain to compare two single names, Santiago and Brett, the male names of the Hispanic and the white group, by filtering on name instead of group, and ask yourself why a gap between two names is more exposed to chance than a gap between two groups. Take the time you need. [advance] The gap between Santiago and Brett is wider than the gap between the groups, on about a hundred replies each. ::: ## A table of the groups {#a-table-of-the-groups .smaller} ::: {.fs-130} ```r by_group <- audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |> datawizard::data_summary(delivered = n(), replies = sum(reply), coded = sum(!is.na(named)), greeted = sum(named, na.rm = TRUE), by = "group") |> datawizard::data_modify(reply_pct = 100 * replies / delivered, greeted_pct = 100 * greeted / coded) |> datawizard::data_arrange("-greeted_pct") by_group ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` group | delivered | replies | coded | greeted | reply_pct | greeted_pct -------------------------------------------------------------------------- white | 308 | 177 | 175 | 107 | 57.47 | 61.14 black | 326 | 198 | 196 | 110 | 60.74 | 56.12 hispanic | 357 | 188 | 187 | 77 | 52.66 | 41.18 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} `sum(!is.na(named))` counts the replies with a greeting code, because each `TRUE` counts as 1. The minus sign in `data_arrange("-greeted_pct")` puts the largest share first. ::: ::: notes A summary is already a table, and printing it is enough while you work. A report needs more: readable names, sensible rounding and a caption. This chain builds one row for each group of names, with four counts and two percentages, and keeps it as by group. The sum of not is na counts the replies that carry a greeting code, because each true counts as one, and the sum of named with na dot rm counts the greetings by name, leaving out the missing codes. data modify turns the counts into percentages, and data arrange, the last of the verbs, sorts the rows, with the minus sign asking for the largest share of greetings first. The white names come first, at sixty-one per cent, and the Hispanic names last, at forty-one. ::: ## A formatted table {#a-formatted-table .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="56%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```r pak::pak("tinytable") # once on each machine report_table <- by_group |> datawizard::data_modify( group = c(white = "White", black = "Black", hispanic = "Hispanic")[group], reply_pct = round(reply_pct, 1), greeted_pct = round(greeted_pct, 1) ) |> datawizard::data_select(select = c( Names = "group", Delivered = "delivered", Replies = "replies", `Replied (%)` = "reply_pct", `Greeted by name (%)` = "greeted_pct" )) report_table |> tinytable::tt() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="44%"} ::: {.fs-70} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Names Delivered Replies Replied (%) Greeted by name (%)
White 308 177 57.5 61.1
Black 326 198 60.7 56.1
Hispanic 357 188 52.7 41.2
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.small} tinytable is not among the packages that the workspaces check. In your IDE the table opens in the Viewer, and one call draws it as a web page, a PDF or a Word document. ::: ::: :::: ::: notes tinytable is the table package of the course, the one to use in your IDE and in a Quarto document, because one call draws the same table as a web page, a PDF or a Word document. It is not among the packages that the workspaces check, so install it once with pak. The chain gives the groups the labels that a reader should read, rounds the two percentages, and keeps five columns under new names, using a named vector as a lookup table for the labels; a name with spaces or symbols in it goes inside backticks. Then tt draws the table. In Positron it opens in the Viewer, on the right of the window, and in a Quarto document it becomes a table of the report, which the last session of the day gives a caption and a number. ::: ## A first figure {#a-first-figure .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```r by_name <- audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |> datawizard::data_summary( share = 100 * mean(named), replies = n(), by = c("group", "name") ) tinyplot::tinyplot(share ~ name, data = by_name, type = "p", flip = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.small} A **formula** says what goes where, the column before `~` on the vertical axis, and a **type** says what to draw. `flip = TRUE` turns the chart on its side. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](r_files/figure-revealjs/r-out-first-figure-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: notes tinyplot draws every figure that you make yourself in the course, and it extends the graphics that come with R, so it needs no other package. The first step computes the six shares, one row for each name, in per cent. Then a plot is one call with two parts: a formula with the data, which says what goes on which axis, read share by name, as in a model formula, and a type, which says what to draw, here points. flip turns the chart on its side, so that the names run down the vertical axis. In Positron the figure appears in the Plots pane. The first draft answers the question but is hard to read: the names are written along the axis, so that only some of them fit, and they come in alphabetical order rather than by their share. ::: ## A readable figure {#a-readable-figure .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```r by_name_sorted <- by_name |> datawizard::data_modify( name = reorder(name, share), group = factor(group, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic"), labels = c("white", "Black", "Hispanic")) ) tinyplot::tinyplot( share ~ name | group, data = by_name_sorted, type = "barplot", flip = TRUE, fill = "by", palette = c("grey60", "#4a78ab", "#8b1538"), legend = list(title = "Names meant to indicate"), xlab = NA, ylab = "Greeted by name (%)", theme = "minimal" ) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](r_files/figure-revealjs/r-out-readable-figure-1.png){width=614.4} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: notes Three changes make the figure readable. The vertical bar in the formula, share by name given group, colours each bar by a third column and adds a legend that explains the colours. The barplot type draws one bar for each row, as long as its value. And the names are sorted by their share rather than alphabetically, which reorder does to the data before the plot. The group becomes a factor first, a column of categories with a fixed order and a label for display, because the palette gives one colour to each level of the factor, in its order. theme minimal sets the look of everything that carries no data. Santiago, at the bottom, drew the fewest greetings by name of the six names, 37.1 per cent of the replies to emails that carried that name. ::: ## Error messages {#error-messages .smaller} ::: {.fs-80} | R says | What it usually means | |---|---| | `object 'audit' not found` | The line that makes the object has not run in this session: run the script from the top | | `could not find function "data_filter"` | The function was written without its package: write `datawizard::data_filter()` | | `there is no package called 'tinytable'` | The package is not installed on this machine: `pak::pak("tinytable")` | | `'data/housing_audit.csv' does not exist in current working directory` | R works in another folder: open the folder of the workspace | | `+` in the console, and nothing happens | An unclosed bracket or quote: press Esc and look for it | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Read the first error first, since the later ones often follow from it. R error messages are terse, and most of them name the thing that R could not find. ::: ::: notes These five messages will be most of what you meet in the course. Object not found means that the line which makes the object has not run in this session, so go back up and run the script from the top. Could not find function means that the function was written without its package, or that the package is missing. No package called means that the package was never installed on this machine. File does not exist in the current working directory means that R is working in another folder, usually because a single file was opened rather than the folder of the workspace. And a plus sign in the console with nothing happening means that R is waiting for the end of a statement: an unclosed bracket or quote. Press Escape and look for it. [advance] The habit that I would most like you to keep is to read the error, starting with the first one. ::: ## The next session and the reading {#next-session} ::: {.small .nonincremental} - **The next session** takes up Positron, the IDE of the course: opening the folder, the panes of the window, running code from the editor, the console and the Variables pane, the Data Explorer, plots and help, and the terminal. Its reading is the module Positron and other IDEs - **The reading of this session** is the module Getting started with R, whose blocks run in your browser. Its second part reads the same data in other formats, fetches the public file of the OAs from the Harvard Dataverse and fits a first model ::: ::: {.urlbox} [[codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html)]{.fs-80} ::: ::: {.urlbox} [[codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/ide.html](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/ide.html)]{.fs-80} ::: ::: notes That is the R that the course asks of you: read a file, look at it, reshape it with a handful of verbs, and compute, tabulate and draw. The reading of this session is the module that you worked through before the course, Getting started with R, and its second part is there for anyone who wants more. It reads the same data in the formats of Stata and other programs, fetches the public file of the original authors from the Harvard Dataverse, and fits a first model. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
